sections.title: CS and AI developments
sections.content:
Video-language models can get the count right without ever building the event history

A new controlled study, The Low Frequency Trap, replaces messy real-world video with three executable tasks: bouncing-ball wall contacts, brief visual blinks and categorical state transitions. Across 2,190 videos, the authors independently vary event count and frequency and score not only the final count but the model’s timestamp-level event trace.

At an 80% reliability threshold, Gemini 3.6 Flash can count persistent state transitions up to 12 events at 0.5–1 Hz, but has no reliable positive-count region for transient blinks. In the high-count/high-frequency regime, only 0.2% of final counts are correct and only 18.1% of true events are recovered. Increasing frame sampling improves one aggregate bouncing-ball score from 19.6% to 29.3%, yet the reported event sequence matches ground truth only 3.7% of the time.

The systems lesson is to keep an external event ledger—event, timestamp, confidence, object/state identity—and compute counts or transitions from that ledger. Final-answer metrics can otherwise reward a correct aggregate backed by a hallucinated history. Paper

Iteration helps LiDAR completion when the missing evidence has coherent geometry

A second study compares a one-shot predictor, a parameter-matched wider predictor and a weight-tied multigrid refiner while independently corrupting LiDAR with contiguous angular holes, point thinning, range attenuation and clutter.

Under contiguous angular removal, iterative refinement beats the wide control by 0.911 mIoU points. Under 75% independent thinning, iteration adds only 0.300 points, while observation-family training adds 5.975 points. Neither fixes additive clutter. The iterative system also costs 10.74 ms / 0.75 GiB per frame versus 6.25 ms / 0.23 GiB for the wide control.

Iteration helps when surviving geometry can progressively constrain a structured hole; broadly missing evidence is more a training-coverage problem, and false evidence needs an explicit robustness mechanism. Paper

sections.title: Technical idea: HyperLogLog turns cardinality into an extreme-value statistic
sections.content:
Suppose a telemetry stream contains billions of user IDs and you only need the number of distinct IDs. A hash set is exact but grows with the population; HyperLogLog (HLL) instead keeps a fixed-size sketch.

Hash each item to a pseudo-random bit string. A long run of leading zeroes is rare, so observing an extreme prefix gives information about how many distinct hashes were sampled. HLL uses some hash bits to select one of m registers, then stores only the largest observed position of the first 1 bit. The registers are combined with a bias-corrected harmonic-mean estimator.

Duplicates cannot increase a register maximum. The original analysis gives a standard error of roughly 1.04/√m; its worked example estimates cardinalities above 109 with around 2% typical error using about 1.5 kB. The trade-off is that the sketch cannot enumerate its set, and arbitrary deletions are difficult because a register does not remember which item created its maximum. Original 2007 paper

sections.title: Non-CS science: Jupiter’s inner large moons may be in a 100-million-year thermal–orbital cycle
sections.content:
Io, Europa and Ganymede are locked in the Laplace resonance. Their coupled orbits continually perturb eccentricity; non-circular motion lets Jupiter’s gravity flex the moons and produce tidal heat. Heating changes viscosity and melting, which changes tidal dissipation, which changes orbital migration: orbit and interior geology form a feedback loop.

A new preprint combines modern astrometry, surface heat flow, tidal response and moment-of-inertia constraints with an orbital–thermochemical model. The joint observations favour a late-time limit cycle established roughly 0.8–2.0 billion years ago, repeating every 95–150 million years. In the model, Io currently dissipates strongly and migrates inward while Europa and Ganymede migrate outward; Io’s mean melt fraction varies around 10–30%, and Europa’s ice shell around 3–15 km.

This is model inference, not observation of a 100-million-year cycle. Its value is a coupled prediction for Europa Clipper, JUICE and prospective Io measurements: ice thickness, heat flux, tidal response and migration should make sense together. Preprint

sections.title: Geopolitics and political economy
sections.content:
• Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are set to sign a joint defence agreement in Jeddah today. Reuters reports almost a year of negotiations, but the exact obligations were not immediately public. Turkey is a NATO member, Pakistan is nuclear-armed, and an existing Saudi–Pakistani arrangement already treats an attack on one as an attack on both. The significant development is the institutional coupling of a NATO power to a Gulf–South Asian security grouping; it is too early to assume every existing mutual-defence clause now applies trilaterally. Reuters
  • The DRC has banned exports of copper and cobalt concentrates, with possible one-year strategic waivers. The order aims to force more domestic processing and retain more mineral value. It is better read as resource nationalism through the value chain than simple withholding: major operations already smelt substantial copper domestically, and earlier bans were softened where capacity was inadequate. Reuters
  • China’s July export surge is increasingly a high-tech story. Dollar exports rose 23.9% year-on-year and imports 27.5%; in the first seven months semiconductor exports nearly doubled and overall high-tech exports rose 40.7%. External demand cushions weak domestic demand, but the larger the high-tech surplus becomes, the stronger the incentive for trade partners to answer with tariffs, price floors and sector-specific restrictions. Reuters
  • Black Sea attacks are again turning Ukrainian farm policy into a global logistics problem. A Russian strike damaged a Guinea-Bissau-flagged wheat ship and killed a crew member; Kyiv says it will support farmers hit by attacks on ports and the maritime corridor. Ukraine’s agriculture minister says alternative routes may not reach required capacity until late August and would cover only about half the disrupted Black Sea volume. The transmission channel is ship risk, insurance, port throughput and finite substitute-route capacity, not only crop destruction. Reuters

sections.title: Marxist fragment: Zetkin on fascism as a mass political problem
sections.content:
“Fascism is the concentrated expression of the general offensive undertaken by the world bourgeoisie against the proletariat.”

— Clara Zetkin, Report on Fascism, delivered to the Comintern Executive on 20 June 1923; English text published in International Press Correspondence. Primary text

Zetkin immediately distinguishes fascism from a simple White Terror imposed by a small officer clique after a defeated revolution. In her account, fascism is dangerous because social crisis lets it recruit a mass following among strata dislocated by economic and political breakdown, including people who might otherwise have moved toward the workers’ movement.

The strategic claim is that repression from above and reactionary mobilization from below are not interchangeable. If the latter has a social base, defeating it requires understanding why it can organize grievances that the left failed to organize. The report predates German Nazism’s seizure of state power and captures an early attempt to theorize fascism while the category itself was still politically unstable.

sections.title: Two philosophy and political fragments
sections.content:
Tocqueville: legality does not prevent tyranny

“A distinction must be drawn between tyranny and arbitrary power.”

— Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, Vol. I, Henry Reeve translation. Primary text

Tocqueville’s point is that tyranny can operate through law. A majority may follow constitutional procedure and still use legislation to dominate a minority; procedure and substantive limits on power are separate questions.

Dewey: “more democracy” does not mean more of the same machinery

“In this sense the cure for the ailments of democracy is more democracy.”

— John Dewey, The Public and Its Problems (1927), Chapter V. Primary text

Dewey explicitly says this is not a call to duplicate institutional machinery that already fails. Modern economic and technological interdependence creates consequences affecting huge populations while the corresponding public remains scattered and often cannot recognize or organize its common interests. Tocqueville fears public power becoming too complete even when legally authorized; Dewey fears a public too inchoate and weak to govern the consequences produced around it.

sections.title: French usage: quand même
sections.content:
Quand même has a core concessive sense: “still / anyway / despite that.” Il pleut, mais on y va quand même. — It’s raining, but we’re going anyway. Je suis crevé, je vais quand même finir ça ce soir. — I’m exhausted; I’m still going to finish this tonight.

It can also add evaluative or mildly protesting emphasis: C’est quand même cher pour un café. — That’s pretty expensive for a coffee. Tu pouvais quand même me prévenir. — You could at least have warned me. Ah, quand même ! can mean “finally!”, “about time!”, or “well, there we go,” depending on intonation. Tout de même is very close and can sound slightly more marked. CNRTL

sections.title: Music corner
sections.content: Three direct recommendations. Open the three-video YouTube queue.

items.label: Classical
items.description: A compact French late-Romantic piano piece from Femmes de légende. The attraction here is not the Shakespeare programme but the music’s concentrated lyrical/dramatic writing: it gives the short-form rotation a real self-contained arc instead of another light encore. France Musique’s live performance is also a deliberate change of scale after the recent run of larger orchestral recommendations.

items.label: Jazz / fusion
items.description: A live band performance with piano, trumpet, guitar, bass and drums, built around a patient harmonic loop that keeps redistributing the foreground between players. This tests a more spacious UK-jazz/fusion lane than the recent compact trio picks: the question is whether the ensemble development is strong enough to stay foreground listening rather than becoming ambience.

items.label: Other
items.description: A percussive acoustic-guitar duet with a very clear rhythmic engine, memorable riffs and quick transitions. It moves the third lane away from recent psych-pop and singer-songwriter picks into instrumental virtuosity without making unusual instrumentation the entire point; the piece has to work through groove, articulation and melodic shape.

sections.title: Unrelated fact: some Greek inscriptions make you reverse reading direction every line
sections.content:
A late-6th-century BCE lead jumping-weight from the Sanctuary of Demeter at Eleusis carries a three-line victory inscription carved boustrophedon. The word evokes an ox turning while ploughing: one line is read in one direction, the next in the opposite direction, and on reverse-running lines the letters themselves are mirror-style.

The inscription says that Epainetos won the long jump thanks to the halteres—the hand-held jumping weights used by Greek athletes—and probably continued onto the matching weight of the pair. One object therefore records athletic equipment, a victory dedication and a period before Greek writing direction was globally standardized into the later left-to-right convention. Greek Ministry of Culture

sections.title: Puzzle: the Ross–Littlewood urn supertask
sections.content:
There is an unlimited urn and balls numbered 1, 2, 3, … . During the final minute before midnight, perform infinitely many stages: at time −1 minute, put balls 1–10 in and remove ball 1; at −1/2 minute, put balls 11–20 in and remove ball 2; at −1/3 minute, put balls 21–30 in and remove ball 3; and in general, at time −1/n, add the next ten balls and remove ball n.

After every finite stage n, the urn contains 9n balls, so its population grows without bound as midnight approaches. But every particular numbered ball k is removed at stage k, before midnight. Since every ball has some finite number, there seems to be no ball left at midnight.

Question: how many balls are in the urn at midnight? More importantly, identify exactly which limiting inference fails if you think “9n tends to infinity, therefore the final urn must contain infinitely many balls.” What object is taking the limit: the cardinalities, or the membership of the sets themselves? Background
